extracted.subtask_description: A Popular Science Monthly magazine exposition covering (1) experimental and interpretive principles of spectroscopy (molecular/stellar applications) and (2) the origin and historical development of life insurance and mortality tables. Aimed to explain methods, laws, and historical practice to a general intelligent readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absorption-band shift on molecular combination
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of a new (heavier) molecule to a molecule with known spectrum is equivalent to an increase of mass of the other, which lengthens the period of vibration and increases the wavelength: "I should observe the whole spectrum shifting toward the red" (example: Bunsen's didymium salts where bands vary slightly in position with different salts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparison of spectra of related compounds (Bunsen's didymium salts example). The observed direction (toward red) correlates with molecular weight differences; illustrated by reproduced absorption-band figure. Be cautious: full general theory for absorption in media is lacking, so rely on careful instrumental comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solvent (environment) effects on absorption bands
rubrics_metrics.description: Absorption bands of a substance dissolved in different liquids appear but slightly vary in position depending on the solvent: Kundt concluded liquids of high dispersive powers tended to shift bands more toward the red, though no absolute rule holds for all substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret solvent-induced shifts as evidence that some solutions may be chemically more complex than assumed; closeness of chemical affinity between solute and solvent influences amount of shift. Measurements (e.g., Claes for cyanin) should be used and one must avoid asserting a universal law linking displacement to simple physical solvent properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectroscopic thermometry — layer-by-layer observation and control of interfering causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The spectroscopic method can observe separately each layer of the sun and therefore examine temperature "not as an average, but for every part of the solar body"; however spectral changes ascribed to temperature may also be produced by other causes, so one must determine such interfering causes before assigning temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceed by carefully observing spectra in different layers of the sun; if a change is observed at one point, investigate at what temperature that change takes place and whether any other cause could have produced the same spectral change. Recognize that concentration/composition/outer-atmosphere absorption and the corona influence observed radiation and complicate interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-specific investigation of line-intensity variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Line-spectra show curious variations in the relative intensities of their lines that "follow no general rule, and must be investigated separately for each element."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a universal pattern across elements; perform separate experimental characterizations for each element. If particular changes always occur at a fixed temperature for a given element, those changes can be used diagnostically for temperature measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Molecular-environment law (spectra variable with surroundings)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The spectrum of a molecule is in fact variable at any given temperature, and changes if the molecule is surrounded by others of different nature." Placing a molecule in an atmosphere of different nature without change of temperature can produce the same effect as a lowering of temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat spectra as context-dependent: environment (other molecules, atmospheric composition) can mimic temperature-induced changes. Example: lithium shows different lines in dilute vs concentrated spark sources—control for surrounding composition and concentration when interpreting spectra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration/dilution effects on observed spectra
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentration or dilution of the sample (or admixture of a second element) affects observed spectral lines: e.g., lithium's red line appears or disappears depending on concentration; Lockyer noted admixture of a second element 'dims' the spectrum of the first; oxygen and nitrogen lines thin when gases are in small quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using spectroscopic observations (including sparks and arcs), note the concentration of the species and presence of other elements; compare dilute and concentrated samples. Concentration effects can parallel temperature effects and thus complicate thermometric interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spectroscopy to probe molecular interaction forces
rubrics_metrics.description: If vibratory forces (due to molecular vibrations) affect encounters between molecules, the spectroscope can give information about these forces because vibrations influence emission and absorption during molecular encounters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to substitute dissimilar molecules for similar ones and observe any change in spectra; theoretical considerations suggest differences in vibration phase relationships will alter average interaction effects—empirical tests are required to decide actual spectral changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life-insurance foundational principle: law of mortality
rubrics_metrics.description: Life insurance is based upon the theory that there is a law of mortality governing life: "at all ages... a certain proportion of individuals will die during fixed periods." Individual lifespans cannot be predicted precisely, but ratios in large aggregates remain stable under similar conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that insurance pricing/arrangements must rest on aggregate mortality regularities (law of averages and probabilities). Historical development required mathematical and statistical maturity to apply these principles practically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mortality-table construction requires reliable vital records
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing a mortality table requires accurate records of births and deaths with ages (Halley used Breslau registers for 1687–1691); Halley's table began with a cohort of 1,000 and tabulated survivors at each age to compute annual death probabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure data completeness (births/deaths with ages) across a representative population span before constructing tables; compute survival counts and derive yearly death probabilities (example: probability of dying in first year = deaths/initial cohort). Recognize limitations if data sparse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply probability/mathematical methods to annuities and pricing
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of chances/probability should be applied to practical questions such as pricing life-annuities; De Witt demonstrated that failing to distinguish ages when selling life-annuities is fallacious and constructed a mortality-table to address age distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mathematical principles (probability theory) to differentiate pricing by age and to construct mortality tables for correct valuation of annuities and life-insurance products. Historical examples show the value of applying theory to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish annuity and tontine product forms and their implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Different forms exist — tontine annuities (survivor payouts increasing as membership declines), terminable annuities (redeemable after fixed years), perpetual annuities (interest forever, principal never repaid) — each has distinct financial and social implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing life-insurance/annuity schemes, identify the product form (tontine/terminable/perpetual), understand distribution mechanics and incentives, and be aware of historical abuses (e.g., tontines becoming lottery-like).
